To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prolonged epileptic seizures in the baboon cause ischemic cell change, which occurs in the neocortex, cerebellum and hippocampus.

the neuronal alterations typical of ischemia are seen in the brain of primates following prolonged seizures, and that they appear to originate during the second phase when hyperpyrexial, hypoglycemic, hypotensive, hypoxic, and acidotic states are characteristic.

the brain damage seen after prolonged epileptic seizures in baboons was ischemic in nature and was produced in the second phase of seizures by a combination of hyperpyrexia (and perhaps hypercapnia), arterial hypotension (and perhaps systemic hypoxia), and mild to severe hypoglycolysis (and perhaps acidosis).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the development of brain damage in prolonged epileptic seizures in nonhuman primates.
the study of the effects of prolonged epileptic seizures on the brain.
the effects of prolonged seizures in the primate, with particular emphasis on the relation of the ictal physiological changes to the subsequent neuronal changes typical of ischemic brain damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain damage in the baboon model was caused by the interaction of several factors including the epileptic discharge, hyperpyrexia (and hypoglycemic) hypoxia, arterial hypotension and acidosis.
prolonged seizures in baboons are associated with ischemic cell change, which is related to the ictal physiological changes, especially hyperpyrexia.

the ischemic cell change seen in the baboons' brains after prolonged seizures was a consequence of an ischemic insult which originated during the second stage of the seizure and was related to the physiological events which occurred during that stage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ischemic cell change seen in the brain after prolonged seizures was not due to a simple, prolonged, global ischemia but rather to a series of complex, interrelated factors, including the cerebral seizure activity, the systemic effects of the seizure (hyperpyrexia, hypotension, hypoglycemic, hypoxia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, and hyperammonemia), and the effects of the systemic factors on the cerebral blood flow and metabolism.

the neuronal alterations seen in the brain of the baboon after prolonged seizures were similar to those produced in other species by prolonged ischemia, but were not identical with those produced by brief ischemia.

the brain damage in this model is a consequence of the seizure and the accompanying physiological derangements, and that it is a consequence of a prolonged ischemia, not a primary neuronal degeneration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prolonged seizures, in primates, are associated with a variety of ictal physiological abnormalities and these can be related to specific patterns of brain damage.
prolonged seizures in primates, even in the absence of a history of epilepsy or other neurological disease, can cause neuronal damage.
the epileptic activity itself is not the sole cause of the neuronal damage seen in the brains after prolonged seizures.
